**(C)** mitochondria

The TCA (Krebs) cycle runs in the matrix of the mitochondria, where acetyl CoA is oxidised step by step. Ribosomes make proteins, grana are the stacked thylakoids of chloroplasts where the light reaction occurs, and the endoplasmic reticulum is a transport and synthesis network, not a site of the cycle.

**(B)** 36 molecules of ATP

The balance sheet for aerobic oxidation of one glucose totals 38 ATP, which is what a prokaryote gains because everything happens in one compartment. In a eukaryote the 2 NADH formed by glycolysis in the cytoplasm must be shuttled into the mitochondria, and that transfer costs about 2 ATP, so the net gain is 36. Two ATP is the net gain of glycolysis alone, and 4 ATP is the gross yield of glycolysis.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives 36 ATP in eukaryotes and 38 ATP in prokaryotes, while the chapter's table quotes 38 without the transport cost.]

**(B)** Succinyl CoA → succinate

When succinyl CoA is converted to succinate by succinyl-CoA synthetase, the energy of its thioester bond is used to make GTP (ATP) directly from GDP (ADP) and phosphate. That is substrate-level phosphorylation, the only one in the Krebs cycle. The α-ketoglutarate step is an oxidative decarboxylation that forms NADH, succinate to fumarate is a dehydrogenation that forms \(\text{FADH}_2\), and fumarate to malate is a hydration.

**(A)** Glycolysis

Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvic acid, so it is needed only when a sugar is the substrate. Fatty acids are broken down by β-oxidation directly into acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. The NADH and \(\text{FADH}_2\) formed are still oxidised by the electron transfer chain, ending in terminal oxidation, so those steps are not omitted.
